title: Menopause Before 40 Raises Heart Disease Risk by 40 Percent, Major Study Finds
excerpt: A JAMA Cardiology study of over 10,000 women links premature menopause to sharply elevated cardiovascular risk, with blood pressure, cholesterol, and body composition all shifting unfavorably.
body:
• Women who go through natural menopause before age 40 face a 40% higher lifetime risk of coronary heart disease, according to a study published in JAMA Cardiology.
  • Declining estrogen triggers a cascade of cardiovascular changes — rising blood pressure, stiffening arteries, higher cholesterol, and increased visceral fat — that compound heart disease risk.
  • Black women are three times as likely to experience premature menopause as white women, amplifying population-level cardiovascular impact.
  • Experts urge women to share their menopause history with doctors and focus on blood pressure monitoring, cholesterol screening, strength training, and stress management.

Women who experience natural menopause before turning 40 have a 40 percent higher lifetime risk of coronary heart disease than those who go through the transition later, according to a study published in JAMA Cardiology by researchers at Northwestern University.

The study analyzed data from more than 10,000 postmenopausal women across six major U.S. population-based studies spanning 1964 to 2018. The elevated risk — encompassing both fatal and nonfatal heart attacks — held up regardless of race.

How Premature Menopause Reshapes Cardiovascular Risk

Premature menopause, defined as the cessation of ovarian function and menstrual periods before age 40, affects roughly 3 to 4 percent of women — a figure that is higher than the previously cited 1 percent estimate for overt premature menopause.

The mechanism centers on estrogen. The hormone plays a critical role in keeping blood vessels flexible, regulating cholesterol, and managing blood pressure. When estrogen levels plummet, blood vessels stiffen and narrow, forcing the heart to pump against greater resistance.

"Menopause at any age unmasks adverse metabolic profiles: Lipids go up by 20 percent, blood pressure profiles go up, activity levels go down, body fat distribution shifts to the belly, muscle mass becomes lower, and fat mass becomes higher."

— Dr. Priya Freaney, Northwestern University

Dr. Priya Freaney, the study's lead author and a cardiologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, described how these changes compound within a narrow window. When menopause arrives a decade or more early, women are exposed to this unfavorable metabolic environment for far longer.

A separate meta-analysis published in the journal Maturitas, which pooled data from nearly 274,000 postmenopausal women, found that those entering menopause before age 45 had a statistically significant 10 percent higher risk of developing arterial hypertension — a finding that held even after adjusting for age, body mass index, and smoking.

Blood Pressure: The Silent Accelerant

The link between menopause and blood pressure goes beyond simple aging. According to the American Heart Association, women experiencing vasomotor symptoms — hot flashes and night sweats — face an even greater risk of developing hypertension. Those who endure frequent or severe hot flashes over many years are particularly vulnerable.

Research also suggests that women become more sensitive to sodium during menopause, which can further drive up blood pressure. A 2024 review found that postmenopausal women have a significantly higher risk of hypertension than those in premenopause or early perimenopause, and they face elevated cardiovascular event risk even at lower blood pressure thresholds.

Dr. Stephanie Faubion, medical director of The Menopause Society, told Healthline that the hormonal connection is direct. "The connection has to do with the early loss of estrogen, which helps promote heart, brain, and bone health, especially in these younger women," she said.

Racial Disparities Amplify the Impact

The JAMA Cardiology study found stark racial differences. Black women experienced premature menopause at more than three times the rate of white women — 15.5 percent compared with 4.8 percent. While the relative increase in heart disease risk was similar across both groups (41 percent for Black women, 39 percent for white women), the higher prevalence among Black women translates to a far greater population-level burden.

Dr. Rachel M. Bond, co-chair of the Women and Children Committee at the Association of Black Cardiologists, pointed to chronic stress as a real cardiovascular risk factor. "Chronic stress is not 'just emotional' — it can affect blood pressure, sleep, inflammation, eating patterns, physical activity, and how consistently someone can care for themselves," she told Healthline.

What Women Can Do Now

Experts say the findings should prompt action, not alarm. Freaney emphasized that premature menopause occurs before the midpoint of most women's lives, creating a long runway for prevention.

"That should be viewed as an opportunity — the earlier we can implement prevention, the more impact we can have in the long term."

— Dr. Priya Freaney, Northwestern University

Freaney advises 150 minutes of weekly exercise with strength training at least twice a week, since declining estrogen accelerates muscle loss. "Muscle regulates metabolism," she said. "That can counter some of these adverse cardiac changes that occur around the time of menopause."

Dr. Bond recommended three immediate steps: know and control your blood pressure, get regular cholesterol and diabetes screening before symptoms appear, and prioritize physical activity, sleep, and stress management.

The study's authors also argue that reproductive history — particularly age at menopause — should be part of every cardiovascular risk assessment. Traditional risk calculators may underestimate danger for women who experienced premature menopause, according to Freaney.

Faubion added that treating menopause symptoms matters too. "If women are not sleeping because they are having night sweats or mood issues or menopause-related sleep disturbances, this makes it more difficult to do the things that we all know help with heart health," she said.

The findings align with new guidance from the American Heart Association and the American College of Cardiology, which urges at-risk individuals to begin lowering cholesterol as early as age 30.
